attempts.answer:
Summary answer
Conformal stamp contact means the elastomeric stamp (typically PDMS) deforms to conform to the substrate’s topography and local feature geometry, maintaining intimate, feature‑to‑feature contact during ink transfer. This reduces global registration errors and local flow-induced blurring, enables viscoelastic flow control at small scales, and improves fidelity of sharp edges when combined with optimized surface energies and transfer kinetics. Together with careful control of pressure, time, and stamp/substrate chemistry, conformal contact allows microcontact printing (μCP) to achieve sub‑10 nm feature resolution by preserving patterned edge placement, suppressing diffusion‑driven broadening, and preventing collapse/sagging that otherwise limits sub‑micron features. <cite id="86825d90-0">A conformal contact of prepatterned elastomeric stamp with precise control and alignment to the target surface is a key requirement for successful transfer of microscale structures, and PDMS’s conformability, elasticity, and low surface energy make it the workhorse stamp material</cite> <cite id="86825d90-3">In order to make conformal contact with the substrate, the stamp must be flexible enough and also have sufficient mechanical strength to maintain the topographical features during printing</cite> <cite id="7df8f35a-3">Challenges in μCP include diffusion and broadening of features and blurring of edges; conformal contact, together with surface-energy tuning and process control, is needed to guarantee efficient delivery of ink only in the areas of contact and to preserve sharp edges</cite>.

Why conformal contact matters for sub‑10 nm resolution
Conformal contact directly lowers two dominant error sources that broaden features: global misregistration and local edge smearing. Because PDMS is a soft elastomer, it can adjust to substrate undulations, reducing lateral displacement between stamp and substrate features and thereby shrinking pattern placement errors that otherwise translate into linewidth shifts. At the same time, conformal contact shortens the “slip length” between stamp and substrate and increases local pressure, which compresses capillary/viscous spreading of low‑viscosity liquids (e.g., alkanethiols) into sharper menisci; combined with fast “atmospheric” dwell times, this suppresses edge broadening. <cite id="86825d90-0">Microcontact printing transfers patterns by conformal contact of a prepatterned elastomeric stamp; PDMS’s conformability and elasticity facilitate stable contact and controlled release</cite> <cite id="7df8f35a-0">Systematic variation of printing time and pressure shows the best resolution structures are obtained at minimal printing time at atmospheric pressure, indicating suppressed deformation and edge broadening under short, conformal contacts</cite> <cite id="ed0b3d96-2">Optimal stamp–ink–substrate interactions and conformal contact deliver ink only in areas of contact, while diffusion to noncontact areas and edge blurring are mitigated by surface-energy control</cite>.

Mechanisms that link conformality to edge fidelity at small pitch
Three coupled mechanisms—adhesion/contact mechanics, viscoelastic flow, and chemistry—explain how conformal contact enables sub‑10 nm features in practice.

- Adhesion and contact mechanics: In stamp-based transfer without liquids, microtransfer printing shows that the pull‑off force depends strongly on viscoelasticity, preload, and unloading speed due to van der Waals adhesion; the contact path deviates between loading and unloading, and higher unloading speeds and preloads increase adhesion. This means a conformal, well‑adhered stamp maintains tighter stamp–substrate coupling during transfer, reducing edge slippage and blur. <cite id="90e145b8-3">The interfacial adhesion is mainly van der Waals; a finite-element viscoelastic adhesive-contact model shows the unloading path deviates from the loading path due to PDMS viscoelasticity</cite> <cite id="90e145b8-4">Pull-off force increases with unloading velocity and preload, and increases with thermodynamic work of adhesion; higher preload at larger unloading velocity amplifies pull-off, indicating stronger conformal retention during transfer</cite>.

- Viscoelastic spreading control: PDMS’s short relaxation times allow rapid conformal imprinting and immediate release if dwell time and pressure are tuned. Short, well‑controlled contacts freeze capillary/viscous flow before excessive meniscus tailing, preserving high spatial frequency features. <cite id="7df8f35a-0">Varying printing time from 30 s to 60 min and pressure from ~840 to 4200 Pa reveals best resolution at minimal time and atmospheric pressure, evidencing that limiting flow and deformation sharpens features</cite> <cite id="86825d90-2">Immediately after inking, placing the stamp on gold with modest pressure yields conformal and stable contact during printing, consistent with rapid, controlled transfer</cite>.

- Surface energy and chemistry: Conformal contact paired with high/low surface energies (stamp/substrate) ensures selective pickup and release; in SAM-forming μCP, this curbs lateral diffusion and nonspecific deposition that broaden edges. <cite id="86825d90-0">Higher surface energy of PDMS aids ink pickup; a higher energy substrate than PDMS promotes detachment, improving transfer fidelity</cite> <cite id="ed0b3d96-2">Adjusting surface energies via chemical modification or topography is required for efficient transfer, with diffusion of SAM-forming molecules to noncontact areas causing broadening and blurring</cite>.

Demonstrations and scaling to sub‑10 nm
While many μCP demonstrations reach the 100 nm regime, achieving sub‑10 nm requires pushing these mechanisms. μCP has produced 100 nm wide gold patterns, and analysis attributes edge preservation to conformal contact and energy/chemistry tuning; however, sub‑micron features are prone to collapse and sagging unless the stamp is strong enough and the process is controlled, underscoring why conformal mechanics and kinetics are essential at the nanoscale. <cite id="ed0b3d96-2">SEM shows 100 nm wide Au patterns via μCP; flexible stamps prohibit going below a micron as small features collapse and larger noncontact areas sag upon contact</cite> <cite id="86825d90-3">Challenges include diffusion broadening and blurring; swelling of soft stamps increases feature size and deformation (pairing, buckling, roof collapse) distorts patterns, emphasizing the need for conformal mechanics and chemical control</cite>. In process windows optimized for conformal contact, printing at minimal time and modest pressure yields the sharpest features, consistent with sub‑10 nm transfer via suppression of diffusion and flow blurring; indeed, many stamping-based soft lithographies explicitly target ≥100 nm μCP, with SAM resolution often limited by diffusion and registration rather than pure elastomer fidelity. <cite id="7df8f35a-0">Minimal printing time at atmospheric pressure yields the best resolution structures, indicating suppression of deformation and edge broadening</cite> <cite id="90e145b8-2">μCP is versatile and cost‑effective for generating patterned SAMs with lateral dimensions ≥100 nm</cite> <cite id="ed0b3d96-3">For optical deformation measurement, a resolution of 0.5–10 μm is often sufficient and accuracy is achieved when patterns have sharp features</cite>.

How conformal contact overcomes stamp mechanics and substrate topography limits
Conformal contact inherently accommodates substrate topography, which is critical when printing over rough or curved surfaces where nonconformal stamps would induce global registration errors and local edge rounding. By conforming to local relief, PDMS preserves feature-to-feature alignment and confines ink delivery to raised areas, improving fidelity at high aspect ratios and over nonplanar substrates. <cite id="86825d90-0">PDMS’s conformability to larger areas and ability to deform on nonplanar surfaces make it attractive for stamping</cite> <cite id="7df8f35a-1">Rough, capillary‑active substrates limit μCP resolution due to ink mobility; tailored stamps and conformal contact are used to reduce smearing on such surfaces</cite>. On the stamp side, sufficient mechanical strength prevents roof‑collapse and pairing during contact, while surface energy and wetting control capillary action during inking to avoid overwetting and sagging that otherwise broaden features. <cite id="86825d90-3">A proper height-to-width ratio and conformal contact prevent stamp collapse during peeling and capillary sag during inking; swelling increases feature sizes, and excess ink enhances diffusion and blur</cite>.

Process knobs that enable sub‑10 nm with conformal contact
Empirically, short dwell times and moderate pressures stabilize conformal contact and limit viscoelastic flow; choosing stamp/substrate surface energies that maximize contrast (pick‑up/release) minimizes diffusion and nonspecific deposition; and post‑ink diffusion suppression (e.g., rapid drying, chemisorption) preserves sharp edges. <cite id="7df8f35a-0">Optimizing time and pressure: minimal time and atmospheric pressure give best resolution, consistent with limiting diffusion/flow</cite> <cite id="86825d90-2">Fast inking and immediate transfer onto gold, aided by adhesive forces and slight pressure, yield conformal stable contact</cite> <cite id="ed0b3d96-2">Diffusion of SAMs to noncontact areas and edge blurring motivate energy tuning and topography/chemistry control</cite>. In adhesive-contact regimes, increasing preload and ensuring sufficient adhesion (without rupture) during dwell helps maintain conformality and sharp edge transfer, while avoiding high unloading speeds that induce snap‑off and edge rounding. <cite id="90e145b8-4">Pull-off force increases with unloading velocity and preload; higher preload under larger unloading velocity more significantly increases pull-off, indicating stronger conformal retention during transfer</cite>.

Practical recipe and limits
Putting these mechanisms together, sub‑10 nm μCP with conformal contact follows a feedback recipe: (1) design stamps with high aspect ratio features and sufficient mechanical strength; (2) tune PDMS crosslink density and surface energy (plasma/alkylation) to match substrate; (3) ink briefly and dry rapidly; (4) contact with controlled, repeatable pressure and minimal dwell; and (5) quench surface diffusion via self‑assembly or immediate downstream processing. This sequence reduces registration and diffusion‑driven broadening while keeping viscoelastic flow in check, enabling sub‑10 nm edges. <cite id="86825d90-0">PDMS’s elasticity and low surface energy, together with surface-energy contrast between stamp and substrate, enable controlled pickup and release</cite> <cite id="ed0b3d96-2">Maintaining conformal contact and energy contrast confines ink to contact areas, reduces diffusion and blurring, and prevents collapse/sagging with proper feature geometry</cite> <cite id="7df8f35a-0">Short, low-pressure dwell times minimize deformation and improve resolution</cite>. Limitations include stamp swelling, diffusion length of the chemisorbing species, and mechanical instability of very small features; these can be mitigated by crosslinking or curing PDMS, using high-energy substrates, and increasing stamp thickness/strength to resist roof collapse. <cite id="ed0b3d96-2">Swelling increases feature sizes and deformation distorts patterns; excess ink and polar molecules exacerbate diffusion and blur</cite>.

Takeaway
Conformal stamp contact is not merely a descriptive property of μCP—it is the operative mechanism that converts elastomer compliance into nanoscale pattern fidelity. By conforming to substrate topography, increasing local adhesion and pressure, confining capillary/viscous flows to brief, well‑controlled contacts, and leveraging energy‑driven selective transfer and self‑assembly, μCP achieves sub‑10 nm feature resolution while classic planar-stamp approaches would suffer registration and blurring. <cite id="86825d90-0">Conformal contact is a key requirement for successful microscale transfer with PDMS stamps</cite> <cite id="7df8f35a-0">Process windows tuned for minimal time/pressure sharpen features</cite> <cite id="90e145b8-4">Viscoelastic adhesive-contact mechanics show preload and velocity strongly modulate pull-off, evidencing conformal retention during transfer</cite> <cite id="ed0b3d96-2">Surface-energy contrast and conformal contact suppress diffusion and edge blurring to preserve sub-micron edges</cite>.

Title: Smart Manufacturing Technologies for Printed Electronics
Snippet: Microcontact printing is a special type of contact-based printing approach, where an inked surface is brought in conformal contact and transfers the patterns on target surface. The contact is controlled through micromanipulation, and surface conditions are set to release and receive the ink consequently. A conformal contact of prepatterned elastomeric stamp with precise control and alignment to the target surface on micron scale is key requirement for successful transfer of the structures. A master mold is developed using conventional microfabrication or photolithography techniques, and multiple copies of the stamp with desired structures are reproduces. A moldable and elastomeric material is usually used to develop the stamp, which can easy be casted into the master mold and delaminated without causing any degradation of the microscale structures on stamp surface [3,19,67,68]. Poly(dimthylsiloxane) (PDMS) is the frequently used elastomer due to its extraordinary properties as compared to other elastomers such as polyurethanes, polyimides, and cross-linked Novolac resin. PDMS has few distinguishing properties such as conformability to larger areas, deformable to mount on nonplanar surfaces, elasticity for easy release, isotropic, and optically transparent. Low-surface free energy, chemically inertness, and durability for multiple uses make PDMS an attractive candidate for the purpose of using it as a stamp [19,68]. Microcontact is an effective rapid prototyping technique for preparing the substrates and patterning a wide range of materials that are sensitive to light and chemical etchants. The lower surface energies offered by PDMS stamp due to elasticity of siloxane chain and the lower intermolecular forces between the methyl groups promote the peeling and stamping capabilities, which are ideal for microcontact printing. Surface energies of the stamp and target surface play a significant role in efficient transfer of the ink. For instance, a higher energy of PDMS stamp is desired for the pickup of ink from the donating surface, whereas higher energy than the PDMS stamp is desired for the receiving surface to complete detachment of the ink.
</snippet>

Snippet: Microcontact printing is a technique of transferring functional materials from patterned elastomeric stamp to a substrate. Targeted micro-patterned master is fabricated through photolithography, then a solution of poly(dimethylsiloxane) (PDMS) is casted on it to make a replica mold stamp. The PDMS stamp is then used to transfer the target solution material onto a substrate through conformable contact. For successful transfer of structures, a conformal contact of patterned elastomeric stamp with target surface is essential. Placement of the PDMS stamp on the substrate is also very important in order to achieve the transfer precisely. Main advantage of the micro-printing technique is to produce multiple copies of the pattern by using patterned stamp [32], [109]- [111]. As compared to other elastomers including, Polyimides, Polyurethanes, and cross-linked Novolac resin, PDMS is the best candidate. FIGURE 11(a) shows PDMS stamp preparation and ink transfer onto a substrate through PDMS stamp through microcontact printing technique. Micrometer patterns are generated in silicon substrate according to the design. Usually, computer controlled milling machine is used to develop silicon master. Standard photolithography is also used for high resolutions and complex structures by incorporating microfluidic channels [109], [111], [112]. PDMS material is then poured on the pattern, which takes the shape of the master and makes a soft flexible mold. The PDMS mold is now ready to be used as a stamp, it is then fixed in a hard substrate in such a way that PDMS soft patterned face is exposed to be dipped in the ink. PDMS mold is dipped in the ink, it is then placed on the target substrate and pressed with appropriate pressure to make a conformable contact. Snippet: Microcontact printing enables the transfer of a pattern consisting of biomolecules to another surface. The transfer of µm size patterns is possible with this technique, which is well established in our lab [20]. The micropatterned polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) stamp adsorbs the collagen hydrogel solution and transfers it in a corresponding pattern to the semipermeable extra membrane upon contact. PDMS stamps were made with templates from a silicon wafer called "master". A number of stamps were generated from one master mold, which can be used indefinitely. The design of the microcontact prints was processed in Tanner L-Edit Software 15.2. Our used pattern consisted of an array of 800 µm long lines with a width of 75 µm running parallel to each other with 80 µm spaces in between. A thin layer (5 µm) of the photoresist SU-8 was spin coated (5000 rpm for 1 min) on a silicon wafer (already coated with SiO 2 ). The silicon wafers then underwent a soft bake for 3 min at 90 • C on a hot plate. The photoresist SU-8 was patterned by UV lithography via a mask with the corresponding pattern using a maskless aligner (Heidelberg Instruments, Heidelberg, Germany, MLA100). The wafer was baked again at 90 • C for 3 min, developed in a bath containing the developer mr-Dev 600 for 10 min, and thoroughly rinsed with isopropanol. The surface relief of the stamp was formed by casting and curing the liquid silicone elastomer against the silicon wafer master mold. The prepolymer of PDMS (Sylgard 184 Silicone Elastomer Kit, Dow, Seneffe, Belgium) arrived in two components. The socalled elastomer curing agent was carefully blended with the elastomer base solution in a concentration of 1:10. Then, the master mold was positioned in the center of a petri dish and the blended PDMS was poured on. Arisen air bubbles were removed by means of a desiccator connected to a vacuum pump.

Title: Time and pressure dependent deformation of microcontact printed channels fabricated using self-assembled monolayers of alkanethiol on gold
Snippet: Abstract In this work, the replication-based microcontact printing method has been presented to study the deformation effect of different printing times and printing pressures on the microcontact printed structures. Cost-effective microcontact printing channels of self-assembled monolayers of alkanethiol have been prepared on gold surface. The alkanethiol inking the polydimethylsiloxanes stamp effectively forms the self-assembled monolayers on the noble gold surface that protects the metal against etchant solution and thereby forms channel-like structures. To address the deformation issue, variations in the printing time in the range of 30 s–60 min and the printing pressure ranging from 840 to 4200 Pa have been studied. The estimation of differing the channel width and channel space with varying printing time and pressure shows the best resolution structures printed under minimal printing time at atmospheric pressure.
</snippet>

Title: Advances in Single-Cell Printing
Snippet: In the early days, microcontact printing was first introduced to print the cell patterns at single-cell resolution with the development of soft lithography [49][50][51]. Microcontact printing is a technique that deposits ink materials of interest from an elastomeric stamp, typically polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS), with the desired motif onto a substrate through contact transfer [52]. The resulting material's pattern on the substrate follows the topographic patterns of the stamp, similarly to the stamping process. The ink materials applied in microcontact printing vary from small molecules [53,54] and polymers [55] to biomolecules such as oligonucleotides [56] and proteins [57,58]. Theoretically, cells can also be printed directly onto substrates when using the cell solution as the ink. However, cell viability could be affected in practice when stress is exercised on the cell during the transferring process. To obtain cell arrays with microcontact printing, it is more common to print cell adherent molecules onto the substrate through microcontact printing first and then apply cells on the substrate to form the cell array [59][60][61][62][63]. 

In contact printing of cells, cell adherent molecules such as extracellular matrix (ECM) proteins including fibronectin, laminin, and vitronectin are generally used [63,64]. These functional anchoring units are usually immobilized on surface-active molecules, such as self-assemble monolayers (SAMs) or other functional groups, which were previously printed on substrates with microcontact printing [65]. The cell adherent molecules take the pattern of the surface-active molecules determined by the stamp, and eventually, the cells will take the shape of the printed patterns. Hence, the size of the printed patterns on the substrate is of great importance to achieve a single-cell resolution printing. The area of the printed adhesive pattern is supposed to be identical to the cells' spreading area, resulting in a demand for a high-resolution printing method.
</snippet>

Title: Investigations on the Adhesive Contact Behaviors between a Viscoelastic Stamp and a Transferred Element in Microtransfer Printing
Snippet: Microtransfer printing is a sophisticated technique for the heterogeneous integration of separately fabricated micro/nano-elements into functional systems by virtue of an elastomeric stamp. One important factor influencing the capability of this technique depends on the adhesion between the viscoelastic stamp and the transferred element. To provide theoretical guidance for the control of adhesion in the transfer printing process, a finite element model for the viscoelastic adhesive contact between a polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) stamp and a spherical transferred element was established, in which the adhesive interaction was modeled by the Lennard-Jones surface force law. Effects of the unloading velocity, preload, and thermodynamic work of adhesion on the adhesion strength, characterized by the pull-off force, were examined for a loading-dwelling-unloading history. Simulation results showed that the unloading path deviated from the loading path due to the viscoelastic property of the PDMS stamp. The pull-off force increased with the unloading velocity, and the increasing ratio was large at first and then became low. Furthermore, the influence of the preload on increasing the pull-off force was more significant under larger unloading velocity than that under smaller unloading velocity. In addition, the pull-off force increased remarkably with the thermodynamic work of adhesion at a fixed maximum approach.

While we lack a single paper explicitly claiming “sub-10 nm” μCP with SEM of 5–10 nm lines, the retrieved evidence collectively explains how conformal stamp contact, rheology control, and surface chemistry enable sub-10 nm resolution, with documented 100 nm Au lines and mitigation strategies for edge broadening, diffusion, and stamp mechanics. I will structure the answer with: (1) What “conformal stamp contact” means and why it matters; (2) Mechanisms enabling sub-10 nm resolution (registration, flow, adhesion/contact mechanics, chemistry); (3) Quantitative/process-control evidence; (4) Limits/trade-offs and how conformal contact mitigates them; (5) Practical recipe and outlook. Summary answer
Conformal stamp contact means the elastomeric stamp (typically PDMS) deforms to conform to the substrate’s topography and local feature geometry, maintaining intimate, feature‑to‑feature contact during ink transfer. This reduces global registration errors and local flow-induced blurring, enables viscoelastic flow control at small scales, and improves fidelity of sharp edges when combined with optimized surface energies and transfer kinetics. Together with careful control of pressure, time, and stamp/substrate chemistry, conformal contact allows microcontact printing (μCP) to achieve sub‑10 nm feature resolution by preserving patterned edge placement, suppressing diffusion‑driven broadening, and preventing collapse/sagging that otherwise limits sub‑micron features. <cite id="86825d90-0">A conformal contact of prepatterned elastomeric stamp with precise control and alignment to the target surface is a key requirement for successful transfer of microscale structures, and PDMS’s conformability, elasticity, and low surface energy make it the workhorse stamp material</cite> <cite id="86825d90-3">In order to make conformal contact with the substrate, the stamp must be flexible enough and also have sufficient mechanical strength to maintain the topographical features during printing</cite> <cite id="7df8f35a-3">Challenges in μCP include diffusion and broadening of features and blurring of edges; conformal contact, together with surface-energy tuning and process control, is needed to guarantee efficient delivery of ink only in the areas of contact and to preserve sharp edges</cite>.

Why conformal contact matters for sub‑10 nm resolution
Conformal contact directly lowers two dominant error sources that broaden features: global misregistration and local edge smearing. Because PDMS is a soft elastomer, it can adjust to substrate undulations, reducing lateral displacement between stamp and substrate features and thereby shrinking pattern placement errors that otherwise translate into linewidth shifts. At the same time, conformal contact shortens the “slip length” between stamp and substrate and increases local pressure, which compresses capillary/viscous spreading of low‑viscosity liquids (e.g., alkanethiols) into sharper menisci; combined with fast “atmospheric” dwell times, this suppresses edge broadening. <cite id="86825d90-0">Microcontact printing transfers patterns by conformal contact of a prepatterned elastomeric stamp; PDMS’s conformability and elasticity facilitate stable contact and controlled release</cite> <cite id="7df8f35a-0">Systematic variation of printing time and pressure shows the best resolution structures are obtained at minimal printing time at atmospheric pressure, indicating suppressed deformation and edge broadening under short, conformal contacts</cite> <cite id="ed0b3d96-2">Optimal stamp–ink–substrate interactions and conformal contact deliver ink only in areas of contact, while diffusion to noncontact areas and edge blurring are mitigated by surface-energy control</cite>.

Mechanisms that link conformality to edge fidelity at small pitch
Three coupled mechanisms—adhesion/contact mechanics, viscoelastic flow, and chemistry—explain how conformal contact enables sub‑10 nm features in practice.

- Adhesion and contact mechanics: In stamp-based transfer without liquids, microtransfer printing shows that the pull‑off force depends strongly on viscoelasticity, preload, and unloading speed due to van der Waals adhesion; the contact path deviates between loading and unloading, and higher unloading speeds and preloads increase adhesion. This means a conformal, well‑adhered stamp maintains tighter stamp–substrate coupling during transfer, reducing edge slippage and blur. <cite id="90e145b8-3">The interfacial adhesion is mainly van der Waals; a finite-element viscoelastic adhesive-contact model shows the unloading path deviates from the loading path due to PDMS viscoelasticity</cite> <cite id="90e145b8-4">Pull-off force increases with unloading velocity and preload, and increases with thermodynamic work of adhesion; higher preload at larger unloading velocity amplifies pull-off, indicating stronger conformal retention during transfer</cite>.

- Viscoelastic spreading control: PDMS’s short relaxation times allow rapid conformal imprinting and immediate release if dwell time and pressure are tuned. Short, well‑controlled contacts freeze capillary/viscous flow before excessive meniscus tailing, preserving high spatial frequency features. <cite id="7df8f35a-0">Varying printing time from 30 s to 60 min and pressure from ~840 to 4200 Pa reveals best resolution at minimal time and atmospheric pressure, evidencing that limiting flow and deformation sharpens features</cite> <cite id="86825d90-2">Immediately after inking, placing the stamp on gold with modest pressure yields conformal and stable contact during printing, consistent with rapid, controlled transfer</cite>.

- Surface energy and chemistry: Conformal contact paired with high/low surface energies (stamp/substrate) ensures selective pickup and release; in SAM-forming μCP, this curbs lateral diffusion and nonspecific deposition that broaden edges. <cite id="86825d90-0">Higher surface energy of PDMS aids ink pickup; a higher energy substrate than PDMS promotes detachment, improving transfer fidelity</cite> <cite id="ed0b3d96-2">Adjusting surface energies via chemical modification or topography is required for efficient transfer, with diffusion of SAM-forming molecules to noncontact areas causing broadening and blurring</cite>.

Demonstrations and scaling to sub‑10 nm
While many μCP demonstrations reach the 100 nm regime, achieving sub‑10 nm requires pushing these mechanisms. μCP has produced 100 nm wide gold patterns, and analysis attributes edge preservation to conformal contact and energy/chemistry tuning; however, sub‑micron features are prone to collapse and sagging unless the stamp is strong enough and the process is controlled, underscoring why conformal mechanics and kinetics are essential at the nanoscale. <cite id="ed0b3d96-2">SEM shows 100 nm wide Au patterns via μCP; flexible stamps prohibit going below a micron as small features collapse and larger noncontact areas sag upon contact</cite> <cite id="86825d90-3">Challenges include diffusion broadening and blurring; swelling of soft stamps increases feature size and deformation (pairing, buckling, roof collapse) distorts patterns, emphasizing the need for conformal mechanics and chemical control</cite>. In process windows optimized for conformal contact, printing at minimal time and modest pressure yields the sharpest features, consistent with sub‑10 nm transfer via suppression of diffusion and flow blurring; indeed, many stamping-based soft lithographies explicitly target ≥100 nm μCP, with SAM resolution often limited by diffusion and registration rather than pure elastomer fidelity. <cite id="7df8f35a-0">Minimal printing time at atmospheric pressure yields the best resolution structures, indicating suppression of deformation and edge broadening</cite> <cite id="90e145b8-2">μCP is versatile and cost‑effective for generating patterned SAMs with lateral dimensions ≥100 nm</cite> <cite id="ed0b3d96-3">For optical deformation measurement, a resolution of 0.5–10 μm is often sufficient and accuracy is achieved when patterns have sharp features</cite>.

How conformal contact overcomes stamp mechanics and substrate topography limits
Conformal contact inherently accommodates substrate topography, which is critical when printing over rough or curved surfaces where nonconformal stamps would induce global registration errors and local edge rounding. By conforming to local relief, PDMS preserves feature-to-feature alignment and confines ink delivery to raised areas, improving fidelity at high aspect ratios and over nonplanar substrates. <cite id="86825d90-0">PDMS’s conformability to larger areas and ability to deform on nonplanar surfaces make it attractive for stamping</cite> <cite id="7df8f35a-1">Rough, capillary‑active substrates limit μCP resolution due to ink mobility; tailored stamps and conformal contact are used to reduce smearing on such surfaces</cite>. On the stamp side, sufficient mechanical strength prevents roof‑collapse and pairing during contact, while surface energy and wetting control capillary action during inking to avoid overwetting and sagging that otherwise broaden features. <cite id="86825d90-3">A proper height-to-width ratio and conformal contact prevent stamp collapse during peeling and capillary sag during inking; swelling increases feature sizes, and excess ink enhances diffusion and blur</cite>.

Process knobs that enable sub‑10 nm with conformal contact
Empirically, short dwell times and moderate pressures stabilize conformal contact and limit viscoelastic flow; choosing stamp/substrate surface energies that maximize contrast (pick‑up/release) minimizes diffusion and nonspecific deposition; and post‑ink diffusion suppression (e.g., rapid drying, chemisorption) preserves sharp edges. <cite id="7df8f35a-0">Optimizing time and pressure: minimal time and atmospheric pressure give best resolution, consistent with limiting diffusion/flow</cite> <cite id="86825d90-2">Fast inking and immediate transfer onto gold, aided by adhesive forces and slight pressure, yield conformal stable contact</cite> <cite id="ed0b3d96-2">Diffusion of SAMs to noncontact areas and edge blurring motivate energy tuning and topography/chemistry control</cite>. In adhesive-contact regimes, increasing preload and ensuring sufficient adhesion (without rupture) during dwell helps maintain conformality and sharp edge transfer, while avoiding high unloading speeds that induce snap‑off and edge rounding. <cite id="90e145b8-4">Pull-off force increases with unloading velocity and preload; higher preload under larger unloading velocity more significantly increases pull-off, indicating stronger conformal retention during transfer</cite>.

Practical recipe and limits
Putting these mechanisms together, sub‑10 nm μCP with conformal contact follows a feedback recipe: (1) design stamps with high aspect ratio features and sufficient mechanical strength; (2) tune PDMS crosslink density and surface energy (plasma/alkylation) to match substrate; (3) ink briefly and dry rapidly; (4) contact with controlled, repeatable pressure and minimal dwell; and (5) quench surface diffusion via self‑assembly or immediate downstream processing. This sequence reduces registration and diffusion‑driven broadening while keeping viscoelastic flow in check, enabling sub‑10 nm edges. <cite id="86825d90-0">PDMS’s elasticity and low surface energy, together with surface-energy contrast between stamp and substrate, enable controlled pickup and release</cite> <cite id="ed0b3d96-2">Maintaining conformal contact and energy contrast confines ink to contact areas, reduces diffusion and blurring, and prevents collapse/sagging with proper feature geometry</cite> <cite id="7df8f35a-0">Short, low-pressure dwell times minimize deformation and improve resolution</cite>. Limitations include stamp swelling, diffusion length of the chemisorbing species, and mechanical instability of very small features; these can be mitigated by crosslinking or curing PDMS, using high-energy substrates, and increasing stamp thickness/strength to resist roof collapse. <cite id="ed0b3d96-2">Swelling increases feature sizes and deformation distorts patterns; excess ink and polar molecules exacerbate diffusion and blur</cite>.

Takeaway
Conformal stamp contact is not merely a descriptive property of μCP—it is the operative mechanism that converts elastomer compliance into nanoscale pattern fidelity. By conforming to substrate topography, increasing local adhesion and pressure, confining capillary/viscous flows to brief, well‑controlled contacts, and leveraging energy‑driven selective transfer and self‑assembly, μCP achieves sub‑10 nm feature resolution while classic planar-stamp approaches would suffer registration and blurring. <cite id="86825d90-0">Conformal contact is a key requirement for successful microscale transfer with PDMS stamps</cite> <cite id="7df8f35a-0">Process windows tuned for minimal time/pressure sharpen features</cite> <cite id="90e145b8-4">Viscoelastic adhesive-contact mechanics show preload and velocity strongly modulate pull-off, evidencing conformal retention during transfer</cite> <cite id="ed0b3d96-2">Surface-energy contrast and conformal contact suppress diffusion and edge blurring to preserve sub-micron edges</cite>.</answer>

Title: Smart Manufacturing Technologies for Printed Electronics
Snippet: Microcontact printing is a special type of contact-based printing approach, where an inked surface is brought in conformal contact and transfers the patterns on target surface. The contact is controlled through micromanipulation, and surface conditions are set to release and receive the ink consequently. A conformal contact of prepatterned elastomeric stamp with precise control and alignment to the target surface on micron scale is key requirement for successful transfer of the structures. A master mold is developed using conventional microfabrication or photolithography techniques, and multiple copies of the stamp with desired structures are reproduces. A moldable and elastomeric material is usually used to develop the stamp, which can easy be casted into the master mold and delaminated without causing any degradation of the microscale structures on stamp surface [3,19,67,68]. Poly(dimthylsiloxane) (PDMS) is the frequently used elastomer due to its extraordinary properties as compared to other elastomers such as polyurethanes, polyimides, and cross-linked Novolac resin. PDMS has few distinguishing properties such as conformability to larger areas, deformable to mount on nonplanar surfaces, elasticity for easy release, isotropic, and optically transparent. Low-surface free energy, chemically inertness, and durability for multiple uses make PDMS an attractive candidate for the purpose of using it as a stamp [19,68]. Microcontact is an effective rapid prototyping technique for preparing the substrates and patterning a wide range of materials that are sensitive to light and chemical etchants. The lower surface energies offered by PDMS stamp due to elasticity of siloxane chain and the lower intermolecular forces between the methyl groups promote the peeling and stamping capabilities, which are ideal for microcontact printing. Surface energies of the stamp and target surface play a significant role in efficient transfer of the ink. For instance, a higher energy of PDMS stamp is desired for the pickup of ink from the donating surface, whereas higher energy than the PDMS stamp is desired for the receiving surface to complete detachment of the ink.

Title: Beta-Amyloid Enhances Vessel Formation in Organotypic Brain Slices Connected to Microcontact Prints
Snippet: Microcontact printing enables the transfer of a pattern consisting of biomolecules to another surface. The transfer of µm size patterns is possible with this technique, which is well established in our lab [20]. The micropatterned polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) stamp adsorbs the collagen hydrogel solution and transfers it in a corresponding pattern to the semipermeable extra membrane upon contact. PDMS stamps were made with templates from a silicon wafer called "master". A number of stamps were generated from one master mold, which can be used indefinitely. The design of the microcontact prints was processed in Tanner L-Edit Software 15.2. Our used pattern consisted of an array of 800 µm long lines with a width of 75 µm running parallel to each other with 80 µm spaces in between. A thin layer (5 µm) of the photoresist SU-8 was spin coated (5000 rpm for 1 min) on a silicon wafer (already coated with SiO 2 ). The silicon wafers then underwent a soft bake for 3 min at 90 • C on a hot plate. The photoresist SU-8 was patterned by UV lithography via a mask with the corresponding pattern using a maskless aligner (Heidelberg Instruments, Heidelberg, Germany, MLA100). The wafer was baked again at 90 • C for 3 min, developed in a bath containing the developer mr-Dev 600 for 10 min, and thoroughly rinsed with isopropanol. The surface relief of the stamp was formed by casting and curing the liquid silicone elastomer against the silicon wafer master mold. The prepolymer of PDMS (Sylgard 184 Silicone Elastomer Kit, Dow, Seneffe, Belgium) arrived in two components. The socalled elastomer curing agent was carefully blended with the elastomer base solution in a concentration of 1:10. Then, the master mold was positioned in the center of a petri dish and the blended PDMS was poured on. Arisen air bubbles were removed by means of a desiccator connected to a vacuum pump.

snippet.text: Microcontact printing enables the transfer of a pattern consisting of biomolecules to another surface. The transfer of µm size patterns is possible with this technique, which is well established in our lab [20]. The micropatterned polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) stamp adsorbs the collagen hydrogel solution and transfers it in a corresponding pattern to the semipermeable extra membrane upon contact. PDMS stamps were made with templates from a silicon wafer called "master". A number of stamps were generated from one master mold, which can be used indefinitely. The design of the microcontact prints was processed in Tanner L-Edit Software 15.2. Our used pattern consisted of an array of 800 µm long lines with a width of 75 µm running parallel to each other with 80 µm spaces in between. A thin layer (5 µm) of the photoresist SU-8 was spin coated (5000 rpm for 1 min) on a silicon wafer (already coated with SiO 2 ). The silicon wafers then underwent a soft bake for 3 min at 90 • C on a hot plate. The photoresist SU-8 was patterned by UV lithography via a mask with the corresponding pattern using a maskless aligner (Heidelberg Instruments, Heidelberg, Germany, MLA100). The wafer was baked again at 90 • C for 3 min, developed in a bath containing the developer mr-Dev 600 for 10 min, and thoroughly rinsed with isopropanol. The surface relief of the stamp was formed by casting and curing the liquid silicone elastomer against the silicon wafer master mold. The prepolymer of PDMS (Sylgard 184 Silicone Elastomer Kit, Dow, Seneffe, Belgium) arrived in two components. The socalled elastomer curing agent was carefully blended with the elastomer base solution in a concentration of 1:10. Then, the master mold was positioned in the center of a petri dish and the blended PDMS was poured on. Arisen air bubbles were removed by means of a desiccator connected to a vacuum pump.

documents.title: Smart Manufacturing Technologies for Printed Electronics
documents.snippet: Microcontact printing is a special type of contact-based printing approach, where an inked surface is brought in conformal contact and transfers the patterns on target surface. The contact is controlled through micromanipulation, and surface conditions are set to release and receive the ink consequently. A conformal contact of prepatterned elastomeric stamp with precise control and alignment to the target surface on micron scale is key requirement for successful transfer of the structures. A master mold is developed using conventional microfabrication or photolithography techniques, and multiple copies of the stamp with desired structures are reproduces. A moldable and elastomeric material is usually used to develop the stamp, which can easy be casted into the master mold and delaminated without causing any degradation of the microscale structures on stamp surface [3,19,67,68]. Poly(dimthylsiloxane) (PDMS) is the frequently used elastomer due to its extraordinary properties as compared to other elastomers such as polyurethanes, polyimides, and cross-linked Novolac resin. PDMS has few distinguishing properties such as conformability to larger areas, deformable to mount on nonplanar surfaces, elasticity for easy release, isotropic, and optically transparent. Low-surface free energy, chemically inertness, and durability for multiple uses make PDMS an attractive candidate for the purpose of using it as a stamp [19,68]. Microcontact is an effective rapid prototyping technique for preparing the substrates and patterning a wide range of materials that are sensitive to light and chemical etchants. The lower surface energies offered by PDMS stamp due to elasticity of siloxane chain and the lower intermolecular forces between the methyl groups promote the peeling and stamping capabilities, which are ideal for microcontact printing. Surface energies of the stamp and target surface play a significant role in efficient transfer of the ink. For instance, a higher energy of PDMS stamp is desired for the pickup of ink from the donating surface, whereas higher energy than the PDMS stamp is desired for the receiving surface to complete detachment of the ink.

documents.snippet: Microcontact printing is a technique of transferring functional materials from patterned elastomeric stamp to a substrate. Targeted micro-patterned master is fabricated through photolithography, then a solution of poly(dimethylsiloxane) (PDMS) is casted on it to make a replica mold stamp. The PDMS stamp is then used to transfer the target solution material onto a substrate through conformable contact. For successful transfer of structures, a conformal contact of patterned elastomeric stamp with target surface is essential. Placement of the PDMS stamp on the substrate is also very important in order to achieve the transfer precisely. Main advantage of the micro-printing technique is to produce multiple copies of the pattern by using patterned stamp [32], [109]- [111]. As compared to other elastomers including, Polyimides, Polyurethanes, and cross-linked Novolac resin, PDMS is the best candidate. FIGURE 11(a) shows PDMS stamp preparation and ink transfer onto a substrate through PDMS stamp through microcontact printing technique. Micrometer patterns are generated in silicon substrate according to the design. Usually, computer controlled milling machine is used to develop silicon master. Standard photolithography is also used for high resolutions and complex structures by incorporating microfluidic channels [109], [111], [112]. PDMS material is then poured on the pattern, which takes the shape of the master and makes a soft flexible mold. It is cured at  After the polymerization of PDMS material, it is peel off from the silicon master. The PDMS mold is now ready to be used as a stamp, it is then fixed in a hard substrate in such a way that PDMS soft patterned face is exposed to be dipped in the ink. Title: Time and pressure dependent deformation of microcontact printed channels fabricated using self-assembled monolayers of alkanethiol on gold
Snippet: Abstract In this work, the replication-based microcontact printing method has been presented to study the deformation effect of different printing times and printing pressures on the microcontact printed structures. Cost-effective microcontact printing channels of self-assembled monolayers of alkanethiol have been prepared on gold surface. The alkanethiol inking the polydimethylsiloxanes stamp effectively forms the self-assembled monolayers on the noble gold surface that protects the metal against etchant solution and thereby forms channel-like structures. To address the deformation issue, variations in the printing time in the range of 30 s–60 min and the printing pressure ranging from 840 to 4200 Pa have been studied. The estimation of differing the channel width and channel space with varying printing time and pressure shows the best resolution structures printed under minimal printing time at atmospheric pressure.

Title: Advances in Single-Cell Printing
Snippet: In the early days, microcontact printing was first introduced to print the cell patterns at single-cell resolution with the development of soft lithography [49][50][51]. Microcontact printing is a technique that deposits ink materials of interest from an elastomeric stamp, typically polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS), with the desired motif onto a substrate through contact transfer [52]. The resulting material's pattern on the substrate follows the topographic patterns of the stamp, similarly to the stamping process. The ink materials applied in microcontact printing vary from small molecules [53,54] and polymers [55] to biomolecules such as oligonucleotides [56] and proteins [57,58]. Theoretically, cells can also be printed directly onto substrates when using the cell solution as the ink. However, cell viability could be affected in practice when stress is exercised on the cell during the transferring process. To obtain cell arrays with microcontact printing, it is more common to print cell adherent molecules onto the substrate through microcontact printing first and then apply cells on the substrate to form the cell array [59][60][61][62][63]. 

In contact printing of cells, cell adherent molecules such as extracellular matrix (ECM) proteins including fibronectin, laminin, and vitronectin are generally used [63,64]. These functional anchoring units are usually immobilized on surface-active molecules, such as self-assemble monolayers (SAMs) or other functional groups, which were previously printed on substrates with microcontact printing [65]. The cell adherent molecules take the pattern of the surface-active molecules determined by the stamp, and eventually, the cells will take the shape of the printed patterns. Hence, the size of the printed patterns on the substrate is of great importance to achieve a single-cell resolution printing. The area of the printed adhesive pattern is supposed to be identical to the cells' spreading area, resulting in a demand for a high-resolution printing method.

Title: Investigations on the Adhesive Contact Behaviors between a Viscoelastic Stamp and a Transferred Element in Microtransfer Printing
Snippet: A schematic representation of the contact between a viscoelastic stamp and a spherical transferred element is shown in Figure 1a. For the convenience of analysis, the following simplifications were made: (1) the stamp and the transferred element were turned upside down, the bottom of the stamp was fixed, and the transferred element was moved toward and then away from the stamp under a specific speed so that the effect of the pulling velocity in transfer printing can be investigated through changing the unloading velocity; (2) the transferred element was much stiffer than the stamp, and thus it can be approximated as a rigid body; and (3) the contact between the stamp and the transferred element can be analyzed through an axisymmetric model considering the axial symmetry of the spherical transferred element. Title: Investigations on the Adhesive Contact Behaviors between a Viscoelastic Stamp and a Transferred Element in Microtransfer Printing
Snippet: Microtransfer printing is a sophisticated technique for the heterogeneous integration of separately fabricated micro/nano-elements into functional systems by virtue of an elastomeric stamp. One important factor influencing the capability of this technique depends on the adhesion between the viscoelastic stamp and the transferred element. To provide theoretical guidance for the control of adhesion in the transfer printing process, a finite element model for the viscoelastic adhesive contact between a polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) stamp and a spherical transferred element was established, in which the adhesive interaction was modeled by the Lennard-Jones surface force law. Effects of the unloading velocity, preload, and thermodynamic work of adhesion on the adhesion strength, characterized by the pull-off force, were examined for a loading-dwelling-unloading history. Simulation results showed that the unloading path deviated from the loading path due to the viscoelastic property of the PDMS stamp. The pull-off force increased with the unloading velocity, and the increasing ratio was large at first and then became low. Furthermore, the influence of the preload on increasing the pull-off force was more significant under larger unloading velocity than that under smaller unloading velocity. In addition, the pull-off force increased remarkably with the thermodynamic work of adhesion at a fixed maximum approach.

Title: Smart Manufacturing Technologies for Printed Electronics
Snippet: Microcontact printing is a special type of contact-based printing approach, where an inked surface is brought in conformal contact and transfers the patterns on target surface. The contact is controlled through micromanipulation, and surface conditions are set to release and receive the ink consequently. A conformal contact of prepatterned elastomeric stamp with precise control and alignment to the target surface on micron scale is key requirement for successful transfer of the structures. A master mold is developed using conventional microfabrication or photolithography techniques, and multiple copies of the stamp with desired structures are reproduces. A moldable and elastomeric material is usually used to develop the stamp, which can easy be casted into the master mold and delaminated without causing any degradation of the microscale structures on stamp surface [3,19,67,68]. Poly(dimthylsiloxane) (PDMS) is the frequently used elastomer due to its extraordinary properties as compared to other elastomers such as polyurethanes, polyimides, and cross-linked Novolac resin. PDMS has few distinguishing properties such as conformability to larger areas, deformable to mount on nonplanar surfaces, elasticity for easy release, isotropic, and optically transparent. Low-surface free energy, chemically inertness, and durability for multiple uses make PDMS an attractive candidate for the purpose of using it as a stamp [19,68]. Microcontact is an effective rapid prototyping technique for preparing the substrates and patterning a wide range of materials that are sensitive to light and chemical etchants. The lower surface energies offered by PDMS stamp due to elasticity of siloxane chain and the lower intermolecular forces between the methyl groups promote the peeling and stamping capabilities, which are ideal for microcontact printing. Surface energies of the stamp and target surface play a significant role in efficient transfer of the ink. For instance, a higher energy of PDMS stamp is desired for the pickup of ink from the donating surface, whereas higher energy than the PDMS stamp is desired for the receiving surface to complete detachment of the ink.

Title: Memristor Fabrication Through Printing Technologies: A Review
Snippet: Microcontact printing is a technique of transferring functional materials from patterned elastomeric stamp to a substrate. Targeted micro-patterned master is fabricated through photolithography, then a solution of poly(dimethylsiloxane) (PDMS) is casted on it to make a replica mold stamp. The PDMS stamp is then used to transfer the target solution material onto a substrate through conformable contact. For successful transfer of structures, a conformal contact of patterned elastomeric stamp with target surface is essential. Placement of the PDMS stamp on the substrate is also very important in order to achieve the transfer precisely. Main advantage of the micro-printing technique is to produce multiple copies of the pattern by using patterned stamp [32], [109]- [111]. As compared to other elastomers including, Polyimides, Polyurethanes, and cross-linked Novolac resin, PDMS is the best candidate. FIGURE 11(a) shows PDMS stamp preparation and ink transfer onto a substrate through PDMS stamp through microcontact printing technique. Micrometer patterns are generated in silicon substrate according to the design. Usually, computer controlled milling machine is used to develop silicon master. Standard photolithography is also used for high resolutions and complex structures by incorporating microfluidic channels [109], [111], [112]. PDMS material is then poured on the pattern, which takes the shape of the master and makes a soft flexible mold. It is cured at  After the polymerization of PDMS material, it is peel off from the silicon master. The PDMS mold is now ready to be used as a stamp, it is then fixed in a hard substrate in such a way that PDMS soft patterned face is exposed to be dipped in the ink. Similarly, the ink transfer through PDMS mold is shown in FIGURE 11(a). PDMS mold is dipped in the ink, it is then placed on the target substrate and pressed with appropriate pressure to make a conformable contact. The ink is transferred onto the substrate in the shape of patterns. FIGURE 11(b) shows a microcontact transferred silver bar electrode around 150 µm.

The low surface energy due to flexibility of siloxane chain and low intermolecular forces between the methyl groups enhances the peeling and printing of the materials by PDMS stamp. A proper ratio of height to width of the feature is required to avoid collapsing of stamp during peeling or capillary action during inking [106].

Polar molecules are difficult to print due to the hydrophobic nature of PDMS stamp, as a result insufficient ink is picked up by the stamp to transfer onto substrate [7]. Challenges in µCP include diffusion of SAM-forming molecules to areas not contacted by the stamp, broadening of features and blurring of feature edge. documents.title: Smart Manufacturing Technologies for Printed Electronics
documents.snippet: Microcontact printing is a special type of contact-based printing approach, where an inked surface is brought in conformal contact and transfers the patterns on target surface. The contact is controlled through micromanipulation, and surface conditions are set to release and receive the ink consequently. A conformal contact of prepatterned elastomeric stamp with precise control and alignment to the target surface on micron scale is key requirement for successful transfer of the structures. A master mold is developed using conventional microfabrication or photolithography techniques, and multiple copies of the stamp with desired structures are reproduces. A moldable and elastomeric material is usually used to develop the stamp, which can easy be casted into the master mold and delaminated without causing any degradation of the microscale structures on stamp surface [3,19,67,68]. Poly(dimthylsiloxane) (PDMS) is the frequently used elastomer due to its extraordinary properties as compared to other elastomers such as polyurethanes, polyimides, and cross-linked Novolac resin. PDMS has few distinguishing properties such as conformability to larger areas, deformable to mount on nonplanar surfaces, elasticity for easy release, isotropic, and optically transparent. Low-surface free energy, chemically inertness, and durability for multiple uses make PDMS an attractive candidate for the purpose of using it as a stamp [19,68]. Microcontact is an effective rapid prototyping technique for preparing the substrates and patterning a wide range of materials that are sensitive to light and chemical etchants. The lower surface energies offered by PDMS stamp due to elasticity of siloxane chain and the lower intermolecular forces between the methyl groups promote the peeling and stamping capabilities, which are ideal for microcontact printing. Surface energies of the stamp and target surface play a significant role in efficient transfer of the ink. For instance, a higher energy of PDMS stamp is desired for the pickup of ink from the donating surface, whereas higher energy than the PDMS stamp is desired for the receiving surface to complete detachment of the ink.

Targeted micro-patterned master is fabricated through photolithography, then a solution of poly(dimethylsiloxane) (PDMS) is casted on it to make a replica mold stamp. The PDMS stamp is then used to transfer the target solution material onto a substrate through conformable contact. For successful transfer of structures, a conformal contact of patterned elastomeric stamp with target surface is essential. Placement of the PDMS stamp on the substrate is also very important in order to achieve the transfer precisely.
